LONDON, England (CNN) -- What recession? Christie's, the famed auction house, this week sold a nearly 36-carat diamond for $24.3 million, which it said was the highest price for a diamond sold at auction. The 35.56-carat diamond dates back to the 17th century. The previous record was a mere $16.5 million for a 100-carat diamond in 1995, Christie's said. "In the midst of these challenging times, we were thrilled to achieve an historic price for an historic diamond," said Francois Curiel, chairman of Christie's Europe and auctioneer for Wednesday's sale. The 35.56-carat Wittelsbach blue diamond, dating to the 17th century, was purchased by international jeweler Laurence Graff, the auction house said in a release. Graff was bidding against Aleks Paul of Essex Global Trading, a professional of Russian origin based in New York, Christie's said. "Known as 'Der Blaue Wittelsbacher' since 1722, it is one of very few diamonds which can claim 17th century heritage, incredible rarity and exceptional beauty." The diamond, mined in India nearly 400 years ago, has been privately owned since 1964. Until 1723, Christie's said, all diamonds worn by European royalty came from India. The diamond has a royal lineage. Christie's traces it thus: King Philip IV of Spain (1605-1665) selected the diamond in 1664 as part of a dowry for his daughter, the Infanta Margarita Teresa (1651-1673). She had become engaged to Leopold I of Austria (1640-1705), who later became Holy Roman Emperor. When she died in 1673, her husband retained the diamond, which was passed on to his heirs. In 1722, the diamond entered the Wittelsbach family when the Archduchess Maria Amalia of Austria (1701-1756) married the Bavarian Crown Prince, Charles Albert (1697-1745). It was worn by successive rulers until the abdication of King Ludwig III (1845-1921) in 1918. The world's largest deep blue diamond is the "Hope Diamond," a 45.52-carat stone housed at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, DC. Diamonds apparently are recession-proof. Christie's reported jewelry sales of $226 million for the first half of 2008, calling it "the best jewelry season ever seen at auction." Sales for the first six months of this year marked a 32 percent increase over the same period in 2007, Christie's said. According to Christie's, key diamonds the company sold in the first half of 2008 included a 13.39-carat fancy intense blue diamond that fetched $8.9 million in Geneva on May 14 and the pear-shaped potentially flawless 38-carat Onassis diamond, which sold for $7.1 million on June 11 in London.

*As economic uncertainty grips global markets, the rarefied world of fine jewelry tells a different story*

---

In an auction room where the tension was palpable and paddles rose in rapid succession, Christie's recently demonstrated that the appetite for extraordinary gemstones remains undiminished—even as broader economic indicators flash warning signs. The record-setting sale has become a talking point among market watchers trying to reconcile robust luxury spending with headlines about recession and belt-tightening.

## A Sale That Captured Attention

The centerpiece diamond commanded a price that placed it among the most valuable ever sold at auction, drawing bidders from multiple continents. Competition was fierce, with the final hammer price substantially exceeding pre-sale estimates. For an item of this caliber—exceptional in carat weight, clarity, and provenance—the result underscored a persistent truth about the top tier of the market: the rarest objects follow their own economic logic.

Industry observers noted that such lots attract a specific class of buyer, one largely insulated from the economic pressures affecting everyday consumers.

## The Two-Tiered Reality

While the auction results are genuinely impressive, seasoned analysts urge context. The strength at the very apex of the market does not necessarily reflect conditions across the entire jewelry sector.

"There's a meaningful distinction between the ultra-high-end auction market and the broader retail jewelry business," industry analysts frequently point out. The buyers competing for a multimillion-dollar stone represent a demographic whose wealth—and spending—tends to remain stable through downturns. Meanwhile, mid-market jewelers and diamond retailers often experience the recession quite differently, with softer demand and more cautious consumers.

## Why the Top Holds Firm

Several factors help explain the apparent disconnect:

**Flight to tangible assets.** In uncertain times, some wealthy investors view exceptional gemstones as stores of value—physical assets that can weather currency fluctuations and market volatility.

**Scarcity dynamics.** Truly exceptional diamonds are finite and irreplaceable, creating a supply-constrained market that behaves unlike ordinary consumer goods.

**Wealth concentration.** The fortunes of the ultra-wealthy have, in many recent economic cycles, proven remarkably resilient, sustaining demand at the highest price points.

## A Measured Conclusion

The record sale is a legitimate and notable data point—a signal that the elite echelon of the jewelry world is thriving. But it would be a mistake to read a single spectacular auction as proof that the entire diamond and jewelry market is booming.

The fuller picture is one of divergence: extraordinary strength at the top, coexisting with more challenging conditions elsewhere. In luxury, as in economics, the headline rarely tells the whole story.
